subsection: A Core European Region: the Paris Basin

notes.b: The Paris Basin is a large, low sedimentary lowland (a basin floored by layers of rock laid down as sediment) in northern France, centred on Paris. Knowing exactly where it starts and stops matters, because the edging hills are not part of it.
points: It is open to the English Channel in the north-west, so the basin has a sea outlet on one side and is closed in by higher land elsewhere.
Older uplands ring the basin and mark its edge, and they are not part of the lowland: the Armorican Massif (west), the Massif Central (south), the Vosges (east) and the Ardennes (north-east).
The basin covers several French administrative regions (the main divisions used to govern France). Île-de-France, the region containing Paris, is its core.
France has 13 regions in mainland France (since 2016); Île-de-France is one of them.
notes.tip: The Vosges, Ardennes, Armorican Massif and Massif Central are the rim of the basin, not uplands inside it. Say they bound the region rather than that they are in it.

notes.h: Why the Paris Basin is a core region
notes.b: A core region is one where people, wealth and decision-making are concentrated. The Paris Basin earns that status from the concentration of people, wealth and functions around Paris, and from the links that radiate out from it.
points: Paris is the capital, so government, finance and head offices (the headquarters of large firms) are concentrated there.
The region holds the largest concentration of population, wealth, industry and services in France.
Fertile farmland surrounds the city and supplies its food, so the city does not depend on distant supplies.
The national transport network is focused on the region, so routes across France lead in and out of it.
The basin has a central position in the EU.
The reasons reinforce each other: the large market draws industry and services, these draw migrants, and the transport links carry goods and people in and out.
notes.tip: Do not use the 'Blue Banana' (the core axis from south-east England to northern Italy) to explain core status, because it does not include Paris.

notes.b: Exams ask for an outline map of a European region with named features on it. These are the items you can draw and name, and where each one belongs.
points: River: draw the Seine and name it; the Marne, Oise and Loire may be added as named rivers.
Urban centres: name Paris with two others from Rouen, Le Havre, Reims, Orléans, Troyes, Chartres or Amiens.

Placement on rivers: Paris, Rouen and Le Havre lie on the Seine, with Le Havre at its mouth and Rouen upstream of it. Troyes is on the Seine upstream of Paris. Orléans is on the Loire. Épernay, not Reims, is on the Marne.
Placement elsewhere: Chartres lies in the Beauce (a lowland plain) and Amiens is on the Somme.
Relief: shade the Beauce (lowland plain) and the Brie plateau, and mark the edging uplands on the rim, labelled as bounding the region.
Agricultural area: the Beauce for cereals, and Champagne for vines.
Industrial area: the Lower Seine between Rouen and Le Havre.
notes.tip: The expected answer is a named river (the Seine), two named urban centres, a named relief feature and a named farming or industrial area. The Beauce is the safest named lowland. Remember Reims is not on the Marne, and Lyon is not in the Paris Basin.

notes.h: Climate: a transition from west to east
notes.b: The climate is transitional, between cool temperate oceanic conditions in the west (mild, wet, moderated by the sea) and more continental conditions in the east (bigger swings between summer and winter). This shapes what can be grown.
points: The annual temperature range (the gap between the warmest and coldest month) increases from west to east, so inland winters are colder and summers warmer.
Paris: average January temperature about 5°C; average July temperature about 20°C.
Paris: annual rainfall about 600–650 mm, spread fairly evenly through the year, so rainfall is moderate and there is no dry season.
Champagne lies near the northern limit of commercial vine growing, so its warm summers are essential to the crop.
notes.tip: Link climate to farming when answering: warm summers ripen cereals and grapes, and the long growing season gives crops more time to develop.

notes.b: The basin is a saucer of sedimentary rock layers, with the youngest rocks at the centre and the oldest at the rim. The resulting low, gentle relief matters for land use.
points: Layers of limestone, chalk, clay and sand dip (slope) gently towards Paris, which sits near the centre on the youngest rocks.
The land is mostly below about 300 m, so the relief is low and gently rolling, which suits large-scale farming.
On the eastern side, resistant layers form escarpments (long ridges with a steep face) that face outwards (east), while their dip slopes (the gentle back slopes) fall back in towards Paris.
Clay vales (low, wet valleys cut in soft clay) lie between the escarpments.
Only the relief and its effect on land use are needed here. There is more on how cuestas (escarpments) form in Landforms from sedimentary structures.
notes.tip: Describe the relief and link it to land use. Do not name individual escarpments, and do not go into how escarpments form.

notes.b: Soil type decides what a farmer can grow, and the basin has a clear pattern: rich loam on the plateaux, thin chalk soil in Champagne, and heavy clay in the vales.
points: Limon, a fine, wind-blown loam, covers the Beauce, Brie and Picardy plateaux.
Limon is deep, fine, well-drained, fertile and easily worked, so it is among the most fertile soils in Europe.
Champagne's chalk gives thin calcareous (lime-rich) soils. The dry chalk plain east of Reims was once called 'Champagne pouilleuse' (poor Champagne).
Fertilisers and modern farming turned that dry chalk plain into productive cereal land, so soil weakness was overcome by human effort.
Heavier, wetter clay soils in the vales and in the west are suited to grass rather than crops, because they are hard to work and waterlogged.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to develop agriculture with reference to two of relief, climate, soils or markets. Limon is the strongest soil example, and Champagne pouilleuse shows how fertilisers improved a poor soil.

notes.b: The Seine and its tributaries (rivers that flow into it) form the main drainage system, and they converge on Paris. The gentle land that makes them useful also makes them a flood risk.
points: The Seine rises on the Langres plateau in Burgundy and flows about 775 km north-west through Troyes, Paris and Rouen to the English Channel at Le Havre.
Its tributaries are the Aube, Yonne, Marne and Oise.
Gentle gradients make the rivers navigable, so boats and barges can use them.
The lower Seine meanders (winds in loops) between Paris and Rouen.
The Loire crosses the south of the region and flows through Orléans.
Permeable chalk and limestone (rock that lets water soak in) store groundwater in aquifers (underground water stores) and give dry valleys, which are valleys with no river in them now.

The gentle gradient and low relief let floodwater spread slowly across the flat valley floor. The Great Flood of Paris (January 1910) and a major flood in June 2016 (which closed the lower galleries of the Louvre) both show this risk.
Upstream reservoirs regulate the flow of the rivers; Lac du Der-Chantecoq regulates the Marne.
notes.tip: Keep Seine details exact: Le Havre is at the Seine's mouth and Rouen is upstream of it. Flooding examples are 1910 and 2016, and upstream reservoirs are the response.

notes.b: The Paris Basin is the main arable region (growing crops rather than keeping animals) of France, and its physical conditions give it a head start in farming.
points: France is the EU's largest agricultural producer and its largest wheat producer.
Low, gently rolling relief allows large fields to be worked with machinery.
Limon soils are fertile and easily worked, giving high yields.
Warm summers ripen cereals and grapes, and the long growing season extends the time crops have to develop.
Dry harvest weather lets crops be gathered in good condition, because wet grain is harder to store.
notes.tip: For the 30-mark question on agriculture, pick two of relief, climate, soils and markets and explain each as an advantage, linking the physical factor to the result in farming.

notes.b: The Beauce is the best example of the basin's arable farming, where flat land and limon soil are put to full use.
points: The Beauce, south-west of Paris around Chartres, is known as the granary of France (a granary is a store for grain).
Crops: wheat, barley and maize, with sugar beet and oilseed rape grown on the plateaux.
Many cereal farms exceed 100 hectares, which is large enough for big machines to work efficiently.
Large, highly mechanised farms achieve high yields on the flat limon land, because flat ground suits big machines.
notes.tip: Do not give farm-size averages or production totals beyond what is stated here.

notes.b: Viticulture (growing grapes for wine) is the basin's best-known specialist farming. It depends on chalk soils, slopes and a protected name.
points: Vineyards lie on the chalk slopes around Reims and Épernay; Épernay is on the Marne.
The vines grow on the slopes of the escarpment, on thin chalk soils.
Only sparkling wine from this protected (AOC) area may be called Champagne. AOC is a legal label that protects a product's name and place of origin.
The Champagne houses (the firms that make and sell the wine) store wine in chalk cellars. Moët & Chandon is based in Épernay.
The houses add value: grapes grown on the slopes become a branded product sold under the protected name, which links farming to manufacturing.
notes.tip: Reims is not on the Marne; Épernay is. Do not give bottle numbers.

notes.b: Where the soil is too wet and heavy for crops, farmers turn to grass and animals. Near Paris, the huge city market favours fresh produce instead.
points: Wetter clay soils and grassland support dairy farming (milk production) in Normandy (west), which produces Camembert cheese.
Brie, east of Paris, is also a dairy area, so it gives its name to Brie cheese.
Market gardening (growing vegetables and flowers for sale) is practised on the edge of Paris.
Proximity to Paris lets fresh produce reach a very large urban market quickly, which matters because fresh goods spoil.

notes.b: Physical conditions are only part of the story. Changes to farm layout, organisation and EU money also explain why the basin farms so productively.
points: Remembrement: after the Second World War, fragmented holdings (many small scattered plots) were consolidated into larger farms.
Mechanisation allows fewer workers to farm larger areas, which is also why the rural population falls.
Farm co-operatives (farmers' groups) and agribusiness firms (large commercial food companies) buy, process and market farm produce.
France receives the largest share of CAP spending (the EU's Common Agricultural Policy) of any member state, which supports French farm incomes.
The Paris market is a large outlet for farm produce within reach of the basin.
notes.tip: Examiners ask about markets as a factor in agriculture, so name the Paris market and remembrement. CAP effects on Ireland belong to a different topic.

notes.b: Forestry and fishing are small activities here compared with farming.
points: Large forests grow on the poorer sandy soils near Paris, which are less useful for crops, so trees took the land. They include the Forests of Fontainebleau (on sands and sandstone), Compiègne and Rambouillet.
These state forests are used for timber and recreation.
Fishing is minor in this region and no port is named for it.
notes.tip: Say fishing is minor and do not name a fishing port.

notes.b: France has few local fossil fuels (coal, oil and gas), so it relies on nuclear power, and the basin's rivers and coast host many of the stations.
points: Nuclear power supplies about two-thirds of France's electricity (recent years).

Nuclear stations sit on rivers and the coast, which supply the cooling water they need: Nogent-sur-Seine on the Seine; Dampierre and Saint-Laurent on the Loire near Orléans; Paluel and Penly on the Normandy Channel coast.
France has few local fossil fuels, so oil is imported as crude (unrefined) and refined on the Seine estuary.
Oil refining and petrochemicals (chemicals made from oil) are located at Gonfreville-l'Orcher near Le Havre.

notes.b: The largest market and labour force in France drew manufacturing to Paris, and firms with head offices and research staff stayed close to it.
points: Market: the Paris region is the largest market in France, so firms locate close to their customers.
Labour: it has the largest labour force in France, so factories can find workers.
Capital: the head offices of large firms and their finance are based in Paris.
Research: universities and research institutes provide the skills and ideas that industry needs.
notes.tip: For the 30-mark question on secondary activity, use two of labour, transport, raw materials, markets, infrastructure and government policy, each with its own explanation.

notes.h: Factor: raw materials and food processing
notes.b: Food and drink processing is manufacturing that turns farm output into products. It sits close to the farms that supply it.
points: Food and drink processing uses local farm output: sugar beet and cereals from the plateaux, and grapes from the Champagne vineyards.
Processing close to the source saves the cost of moving bulky crops such as sugar beet to distant factories.

notes.b: Infrastructure (the roads, rails, ports and other networks that support industry) is a major reason firms locate here. Paris sits at the centre of the network.
points: Paris is the hub of road, rail, river and air transport in France, so firms there are well connected.
Firms can move raw materials and finished goods by road, rail, river and air from a single location.
The Seine and the Lower Seine allow bulk goods to reach factories by water.
Good transport lowers the cost of getting inputs in and products out, so transport links reinforce the location advantage of the region.

notes.h: Car industry and industry leaving the inner city
notes.b: Car making shows both the strength of Paris as an industrial region and a shift in where factories are built.
points: Renault has a plant at Flins, and PSA (now Stellantis) has a plant at Poissy; both are west of Paris.
Renault's Boulogne-Billancourt plant, on Île Seguin in the Seine, closed in 1992.
The closure is an example of industry leaving the inner city for suburban and provincial sites.

notes.b: Between Rouen and Le Havre, the Seine becomes a corridor of ports and heavy industry. It links the basin to overseas markets.
points: The Lower Seine, between Rouen and Le Havre, is an industrial area built around its ports, oil refining and petrochemicals.
Le Havre is France's largest container port, and it sits at the mouth of the Seine where the river meets the English Channel.
Rouen is France's main grain-exporting port, so it links the basin's cereal surplus to overseas markets.
Since 2021 the ports of Le Havre, Rouen and Paris form one body, HAROPA.
notes.tip: Remember Le Havre is at the Seine's mouth and Rouen is upstream of it. Use the Lower Seine as your named industrial area on a sketch map.

notes.b: Modern industry here is based on research and knowledge, and Paris-Saclay is the named example.
points: Paris-Saclay is a research and high-technology cluster (a group of related firms and institutions in one place) on the Saclay plateau, south-west of Paris.
It combines universities, research institutes and company laboratories.
Its research base, such as its universities and laboratories, supports the high-technology firms located in the cluster.

notes.b: Decentralisation means moving activity out of the capital. From the 1950s the French state tried to limit Paris's dominance and spread industry to the provinces (regions outside Paris).
points: Decentralisation from the 1950s–60s restricted new industry in Paris and steered it to the provinces.
DATAR, the regional planning agency, was set up in 1963.
Eight métropoles d'équilibre (balancing metropolises) were named in 1964, including Lyon, Marseille and Lille, to counter the pull of Paris.
The 1965 regional plan (schéma directeur) for Paris led to five new towns: Cergy-Pontoise, Évry, Marne-la-Vallée, Melun-Sénart and Saint-Quentin-en-Yvelines.
Result: because factories were steered away, Paris lost its share of manufacturing but kept its head offices and research.
notes.tip: Lorraine (iron ore and steel) and the Nord coalfield (Lille) lie on the margins of the basin and are regions of industrial decline. Do not present them as the core of the basin's industry.

notes.b: Paris is the primate city of France (a city far larger and more important than any other), and its services are the basis of its economic dominance in the region.
points: Government, finance, head offices, universities and international organisations are concentrated in Paris.
The OECD and UNESCO have their headquarters in Paris, as international organisations that add to its service role.
La Défense, west of the city, is one of Europe's largest purpose-built business districts.
Île-de-France has about 12 million people (2020s), about 18% of France's population (France about 68 million, 2024).
Île-de-France produces about 30% of France's GDP (the total value of goods and services produced).
Concentrated services draw international business, which in turn needs more of the same services, so the centre keeps growing.
notes.tip: Use only the figures given here and do not add tourist totals or GDP per head.

notes.b: Rungis shows how farming (primary activity) and services such as trade and distribution (tertiary activity) connect.
points: Rungis International Market, south of Paris, opened in 1969, replacing Les Halles in central Paris.
It is one of the world's largest wholesale fresh-food markets.
It links primary and tertiary activity: farm produce from the basin is sold wholesale there and then distributed to the city's shops and restaurants.

notes.b: Tourism is a major tertiary activity in the region, with attractions to suit many interests. Heavy visitor numbers also create problems.
points: Visitors come for heritage, culture, shopping, events, theme parks, Champagne and the countryside.
The Eiffel Tower was built for the 1889 Exposition Universelle. The Louvre is the world's most visited art museum.
Notre-Dame Cathedral was damaged by fire in April 2019 and reopened in December 2024. The Palace of Versailles is a major heritage attraction in the region.
Disneyland Paris, at Marne-la-Vallée, opened in 1992 and is Europe's most visited theme park, so it is a major draw for visitors.
Paris hosted the 2024 Olympic and Paralympic Games.
Champagne Hillsides, Houses and Cellars became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2015; the Champagne houses in Reims and Épernay offer cellar tours.
Problems: congestion, seasonal pressure on sites (crowding in peak months), and wear on heritage sites from large visitor numbers.
notes.tip: For a question on tourism, give why tourists come, named attractions such as Disneyland Paris and the 2024 Games, and the problems of congestion, seasonality and pressure on sites.

notes.b: Transport is central to the region's development. The network is built around Paris, with new lines extending it.
points: The road and rail network is radial (star-shaped), centred on Paris, so routes spread out from the capital like spokes.
The Boulevard Périphérique ring road, completed in 1973, encircles the city and carries traffic around it, so through traffic can avoid the centre.
The TGV's first high-speed line, Paris–Lyon, opened in 1981.
The Channel Tunnel opened in 1994; Eurostar links Paris with London, so the region is joined to Britain by rail.
The RER is the regional express rail network across the city region, so suburbs are linked to the centre.
The Grand Paris Express is about 200 km of new automatic metro lines with 68 new stations.
Line 14 was extended north to Saint-Denis Pleyel and south to Orly airport in 2024.
notes.tip: Be ready to explain the importance of transport to the region's economic development, not just list routes.

notes.b: Air and river links add to the road and rail network, and together they keep Paris attractive for business.
points: Charles de Gaulle Airport (Roissy, opened 1974) is France's busiest airport; Orly is the second Paris airport, so air links serve the whole region.
The Port of Paris at Gennevilliers is one of Europe's largest river ports.
Transport links let firms in the region reach markets and suppliers quickly, which sustains the concentration of head offices and services.
The same network connects the basin to the Channel ports and to the rest of Europe, so the region gains from both road and river access.

notes.b: The language of the region is tied to Paris's history as a centre of power.
points: The language of the region is French.
Standard French developed from the dialect of the Paris region, which became the standard because Paris was the centre of government.
Immigrant languages are spoken in the suburbs, because of post-war migration.
notes.tip: Give no figures for language.

notes.b: Religion in the region has changed from a Catholic tradition to a mixed and largely secular society.
points: The region is traditionally Roman Catholic, but church attendance is now low.
The 1905 law separating church and state (laïcité) keeps religion out of government and public institutions.
There is a large Muslim minority, mainly of North African origin.
Secularisation (the decline of religion's role in society) has reduced the role of the church in public life.

notes.h: Culture: politics, sport and the arts
notes.b: Culture covers more than religion and language. Politics, sport and the arts all reflect Paris's role as the centre of France.
points: Politics: France is a highly centralised state run from Paris.
Paris Saint-Germain won the UEFA Champions League in 2025.
Stade de France, in Saint-Denis, was built for the 1998 FIFA World Cup.
The French Open tennis is played at Roland-Garros, Paris.
The Tour de France traditionally finishes on the Champs-Élysées.
Paris is a centre of art, fashion and cuisine, which also draws tourists.
notes.tip: For a question on the culture of a region, draw on religion, language, politics, music and dance, and sport and games.

notes.b: Exams ask for the factors that influenced the development of one urban area. Here each factor is matched to Paris.
points: Site: Paris began on the Île de la Cité, an island at a crossing point of the Seine.

Situation: Paris lies near the centre of the Paris Basin, where the Seine's main tributaries, the Marne, Oise, Aube and Yonne, converge (the Marne joins just upstream of the city and the Oise just downstream).
Transport: the city is the hub of a radial road and rail network and of the river port at Gennevilliers.
Administration: as capital and seat of a centralised state, Paris concentrates government, finance and head offices.
Primary activity: the rich limon plateaux around the city supplied food to a growing population.
Industry and services: the largest market and labour force attracted manufacturing and services, including the business district of La Défense.
Planning: the 1853–1870 rebuilding, the post-war estates and the new towns each shaped the city's growth.
notes.tip: Site means the exact spot (the island at a Seine crossing) and situation means the wider position (the centre of the basin where rivers converge). Give each factor with its effect on Paris.

notes.b: Paris grew in stages, from planned rebuilding in the nineteenth century to suburban estates and regional planning in the twentieth.
points: Haussmann rebuilt central Paris between 1853 and 1870 under Napoleon III, so the city gained wide boulevards, uniform apartment blocks, parks and sewers.
Grands ensembles, large high-rise social housing estates built in the suburbs (banlieues) in the 1950s–70s, housed a growing population; Sarcelles is an example.
Growth spread beyond the Périphérique ring road into the surrounding suburbs.
The five new towns built under the 1965 plan are Cergy-Pontoise, Évry, Marne-la-Vallée, Melun-Sénart and Saint-Quentin-en-Yvelines.
Métropole du Grand Paris was created on 1 January 2016, joining Paris with about 130 surrounding communes (the smallest units of local government in France).
The Grand Paris Express metro network is the latest large-scale project for the city region.

notes.b: Rapid growth and concentration have brought serious problems to Paris and its suburbs.
points: Congestion on roads into and around the city, because so many people and jobs are concentrated there.
High housing costs, which push people out to the suburbs.

Social segregation (different groups living apart) and deprivation in the banlieues: Seine-Saint-Denis, north-east of Paris, is the poorest département (a French county-sized administrative area) in mainland France.
Riots in the banlieues began in Clichy-sous-Bois in October 2005 and spread across France.
Urban sprawl: development spreads outward into the surrounding countryside, because high housing costs push people out.

notes.b: Away from Paris, the countryside has changed as farming has mechanised and as the city's influence has spread outward.
points: Fewer farmers on larger holdings leave the outer basin with a declining rural population.
Rural depopulation in the outer basin forms part of the 'diagonale du vide' (empty diagonal), a band of low population density from north-east to south-west France.
Commuter villages near Paris are growing as residents travel to jobs in the city.
Second homes and rural tourism bring visitors and money to villages in the Champagne and countryside areas.
notes.tip: Do not say exactly which départements the diagonale du vide includes.

notes.b: Population is very unevenly spread: packed into Paris and its region, thinly spread across the outer basin.
points: Île-de-France has about 1,000 people per km² (2020s).
The City of Paris has about 2.1 million people (2020s) on about 105 km², about 20,000 people per km²; it is divided into 20 arrondissements (administrative districts of the city).
Densities are much lower in rural Champagne and across the outer basin, where mechanised farming needs few workers.
The dense core exists because jobs, services and transport access are concentrated in and around Paris.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to account for population distribution in a European region, so give reasons: jobs, services and transport in the core against farm mechanisation in the outer basin.

notes.b: Population change in the basin has been driven by movement of people into Paris, from the French countryside and from abroad.
points: Jean-François Gravier's Paris et le désert français (Paris and the French desert), 1947, argued that Paris drained people and wealth from the rest of France.
Rural-to-urban migration into Paris continued because jobs and services concentrated there.
The Paris region has a young age structure, because in-migrants are mostly young adults seeking work.
Older residents move out of the region on retirement, so the age structure stays young.
After the Second World War, immigrant labour arrived from Algeria, Morocco, Tunisia and Portugal.

keyTerms.definition: A fine, wind-blown loam that covers the plateaux of the Paris Basin and is deep, fertile and easily worked.
A ridge with a steep escarpment facing outwards and a gently sloping dip slope facing back towards the centre of the basin.
The gently sloping side of a cuesta, which follows the direction in which the rock layers dip.
Land used for growing crops rather than for pasture.
A protected designation (appellation d'origine contrôlée) that limits a product's name to wine or food made in a defined area.
The consolidation of fragmented farm plots into larger holdings, carried out in France after the Second World War.
The largest city in a country, which dominates its economy, government and services.
A system of roads and railways that radiates out from one central city like the spokes of a wheel.
Large high-rise social housing estates built in the suburbs of French cities in the 1950s–70s.
The French principle of separating church and state, set in law in 1905.
A balancing metropolis: one of eight cities named in 1964 to counter the dominance of Paris.
A suburb around a French city, often with large social housing estates.

factCards.term: Sketch map of the Paris Basin: what to show and where
factCards.definition: River: the Seine, with Paris, Rouen and Le Havre (at its mouth) on it. Cities: Paris plus Rouen, Le Havre or Reims. Relief: the Beauce lowland, with rim uplands drawn as its edge. Farming: the Beauce (cereals) or Champagne (vines). Industry: the Lower Seine.

factCards.term: Paris Basin: location, boundaries and why it is a core region
factCards.definition: A low sedimentary basin in northern France, open to the English Channel, ringed by the Armorican Massif, Massif Central, Vosges and Ardennes. Core: the capital; France's largest concentration of people, wealth, industry and services; fertile farmland; the transport hub.

factCards.term: Paris Basin climate: figures and the west–east change
factCards.definition: Paris: January about 5°C, July about 20°C, about 600–650 mm of rain spread through the year. Oceanic in the west, more continental eastwards, with colder winters and warmer summers inland. Champagne lies near the northern limit of commercial vine growing.

factCards.term: Paris Basin relief and soils
factCards.definition: A saucer of limestone, chalk, clay and sand layers dipping towards Paris, mostly below 300 m, with outward-facing escarpments and clay vales in the east. Deep, fertile limon covers the Beauce, Brie and Picardy plateaux; Champagne has thin chalk soils; clay suits grass.

factCards.term: The Seine: course, tributaries and flooding
factCards.definition: About 775 km from the Langres plateau through Troyes, Paris and Rouen to Le Havre; the Aube, Yonne, Marne and Oise converge on Paris; gentle gradients make it navigable. It flooded in January 1910 and June 2016; upstream reservoirs such as Lac du Der-Chantecoq regulate it.

factCards.term: Paris Basin agriculture: physical advantages
factCards.definition: Low, gently rolling relief suits large mechanised fields; limon soils are fertile and easily worked; warm summers ripen cereals and grapes over a long growing season; dry weather at harvest. France is the EU's largest farm and wheat producer.

factCards.term: The Beauce: cereal farming in the 'granary of France'
factCards.definition: South-west of Paris around Chartres. Wheat, barley and maize, with sugar beet and oilseed rape; many farms exceed 100 hectares; large, highly mechanised farms on flat limon land give high yields.

factCards.term: Champagne: how and where its vines are grown
factCards.definition: Vines grow on chalk escarpment slopes around Reims and Épernay (on the Marne). Only sparkling wine from this AOC area may be called Champagne; houses such as Moët & Chandon age it in chalk cellars, adding value. UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2015.

factCards.term: Dairying and market gardening in the Paris Basin
factCards.definition: Wetter clay grassland supports dairying in Normandy (Camembert) and Brie (Brie cheese). Market gardening of vegetables and flowers on the edge of Paris gets fresh produce quickly to a huge urban market.

factCards.term: Human and economic factors in Paris Basin farming
factCards.definition: Remembrement consolidated scattered plots after the Second World War; mechanisation; co-operatives and agribusiness; France gets the largest share of CAP spending; the Paris market, served by Rungis (1969, replacing Les Halles); rural depopulation as farms mechanised.

factCards.term: Energy in the Paris Basin: nuclear power and oil refining
factCards.definition: Nuclear power gives about two-thirds of France's electricity, from stations by cooling water: Nogent-sur-Seine (Seine), Dampierre and Saint-Laurent (Loire), Paluel and Penly (Normandy coast). Imported crude is refined at Gonfreville-l'Orcher near Le Havre.

factCards.term: Why manufacturing concentrated in and around Paris
factCards.definition: France's largest market and labour force; head offices and capital; universities and research; the hub of road, rail, river and air transport; government. Food processing uses local sugar beet, cereals and Champagne grapes, saving the cost of moving bulky crops.

factCards.term: Paris Basin car industry and industry leaving the inner city
factCards.definition: Renault at Flins and PSA (now Stellantis) at Poissy, both west of Paris. Renault's Boulogne-Billancourt plant on Île Seguin closed in 1992 as industry moved from the inner city to suburban and provincial sites.

factCards.term: Lower Seine industrial axis and Paris-Saclay
factCards.definition: Le Havre, France's largest container port, and Rouen, its main grain-exporting port, have oil refining and petrochemicals; with Paris they form HAROPA (2021). Paris-Saclay, south-west of Paris, is a research and high-technology cluster.

factCards.term: Decentralisation policy and its effect on Paris industry
factCards.definition: From the 1950s–60s new industry in Paris was restricted and steered to the provinces: DATAR (1963); eight métropoles d'équilibre (1964), such as Lyon, Marseille and Lille; the 1965 plan's new towns. Paris lost manufacturing but kept head offices and research.

factCards.term: Name the five new towns built around Paris
factCards.definition: Cergy-Pontoise, Évry, Marne-la-Vallée, Melun-Sénart and Saint-Quentin-en-Yvelines, created under the 1965 regional plan (schéma directeur) for Paris.

factCards.term: Paris as a primate city and service centre: key facts
factCards.definition: Government, finance, head offices and universities; OECD and UNESCO headquarters; La Défense, one of Europe's largest business districts. Île-de-France has about 12 million people (about 18% of France) and produces about 30% of French GDP.

factCards.term: Paris Basin tourism: named attractions and problems
factCards.definition: Eiffel Tower (1889); the Louvre, the most visited art museum; Notre-Dame (fire 2019, reopened 2024); Versailles; Disneyland Paris, Marne-la-Vallée (1992); the 2024 Olympic Games; Champagne cellar tours. Problems: congestion, seasonal pressure, wear on sites.

factCards.term: Paris Basin transport: road, rail, air and river
factCards.definition: Radial network centred on Paris; Périphérique (1973); TGV Paris–Lyon (1981); Channel Tunnel and Eurostar (1994); RER; Grand Paris Express (about 200 km, 68 stations); Charles de Gaulle (1974), France's busiest airport, and Orly; river port at Gennevilliers.

factCards.term: Population distribution in the Paris Basin, with reasons
factCards.definition: Île-de-France about 1,000 per km²; City of Paris about 2.1 million on 105 km², about 20,000 per km²; far lower in rural Champagne and the outer basin. Reasons: jobs, services and transport concentrate in Paris; mechanised farms need few workers.

factCards.term: Population dynamics and migration in the Paris Basin
factCards.definition: Gravier's 'Paris and the French desert' (1947) argued Paris drained France; rural-to-urban migration gave the region a young age structure; retirees move out; post-war immigrants came from Algeria, Morocco, Tunisia and Portugal.

factCards.term: Culture of the Paris Basin: language, religion, politics and sport
factCards.definition: Standard French grew from the Paris dialect; traditionally Catholic, with low attendance, laïcité (1905) and a large North African Muslim minority; a centralised state; Paris Saint-Germain, Roland-Garros, the Tour de France finish, Stade de France (1998).

factCards.term: Factors in the growth of Paris as an urban area
factCards.definition: Site: the Île de la Cité, a Seine crossing. Situation: centre of the basin, where the Seine's tributaries converge (the Marne joins just upstream, the Oise just downstream). Capital of a centralised state; hub of radial transport; rich limon farmland; France's largest market and labour force.

factCards.term: Urban development of Paris: main planning stages
factCards.definition: Haussmann rebuilt the centre (1853–1870) with boulevards, apartment blocks, parks and sewers; grands ensembles such as Sarcelles (1950s–70s); the Périphérique; new towns (1965 plan); La Défense; Métropole du Grand Paris (2016, about 130 communes); Grand Paris Express.

factCards.term: Urban problems of Paris
factCards.definition: Congestion; high housing costs; segregation and deprivation in the banlieues, where Seine-Saint-Denis is the poorest département in mainland France; riots that began in Clichy-sous-Bois in October 2005; urban sprawl.

factCards.term: Rural development in the Paris Basin
factCards.definition: Fewer farmers on larger holdings; depopulation of the outer basin, part of the 'diagonale du vide'; commuter villages growing near Paris; second homes and rural tourism bringing visitors and money.

questions.prompt: Account for the development of agriculture in a European region (not in Ireland) that you have studied, with reference to relief and climate.
questions.model: Relief: the Paris Basin is a low, gently rolling saucer of land, mostly below about 300 m, which allows large fields to be worked by machines. The plateaux of the Beauce, Brie and Picardy are covered with limon, a deep, fine, well-drained and fertile soil that is easily worked and gives high yields. In the Beauce, large, highly mechanised cereal farms growing wheat, barley and maize, many over 100 hectares, produce the granary of France. Vines are grown on the chalk slopes of the escarpment in Champagne, where thin calcareous soils were once poor; fertilisers and modern farming have made the dry chalk plain productive. The wetter clay vales and the west suit grass and dairy farming. Climate: Paris averages about 5°C in January and about 20°C in July, and its annual rainfall of about 600–650 mm is spread fairly evenly through the year. The annual temperature range increases eastwards, so inland winters are colder and summers warmer. Warm summers ripen cereals and grapes, the growing season is long, and dry harvest weather lets crops be gathered in good condition. Champagne lies near the northern limit of commercial vine growing, so its warm summers are essential. Relief and climate give the basin clear advantages for farming, and the fertile limon soils make the most of both.

questions.prompt: Examine two factors that have influenced the development of secondary economic activity in a European region (not in Ireland).
questions.model: Markets and labour: Paris is the largest market in France and has the largest labour force, so firms locate there to sell to customers and recruit workers. Manufacturing in the region includes the Renault plant at Flins and the PSA (now Stellantis) plant at Poissy, both west of Paris. Renault closed its Boulogne-Billancourt plant on Île Seguin in the Seine in 1992, an example of industry leaving the inner city for suburban and provincial sites. Paris-Saclay, south-west of Paris, is a research and high-technology cluster that draws on the region's universities. Government policy: decentralisation from the 1950s–60s restricted new industry in Paris and steered it to the provinces. DATAR, the regional planning agency, was set up in 1963. Eight métropoles d'équilibre were named in 1964 to counter Paris, and the 1965 regional plan led to five new towns around the city: Cergy-Pontoise, Évry, Marne-la-Vallée, Melun-Sénart and Saint-Quentin-en-Yvelines. The result was that Paris lost its share of manufacturing but kept its head offices and research.

questions.prompt: Discuss the factors which influenced the development of one urban area in a European region (not in Ireland).
questions.model: Site: Paris began on the Île de la Cité, an island at a crossing point of the Seine. Situation: Paris lies near the centre of the Paris Basin, where the Seine's main tributaries, the Marne, Oise, Aube and Yonne, converge (the Marne joins just upstream of the city and the Oise just downstream). Transport: the city is the hub of a radial road and rail network, and the Port of Paris at Gennevilliers is one of Europe's largest river ports. Administration: as the capital of a highly centralised state, Paris concentrates government, finance and head offices, and it is home to the OECD and UNESCO. Primary activity: the fertile limon plateaux around the city supplied food to a growing population, and Rungis now distributes fresh produce to it. Industry and services: the largest market and labour force attracted manufacturing and services, and La Défense became one of Europe's largest purpose-built business districts. Growth and planning: Haussmann rebuilt central Paris between 1853 and 1870 with wide boulevards, parks and sewers; post-war grands ensembles housed workers in the suburbs; the 1965 plan created five new towns; the Métropole du Grand Paris was created on 1 January 2016, joining Paris with about 130 communes; and the Grand Paris Express is extending the metro network.
